Cloud-a-thon @ UH 2026: AI Challenge (Bank Marketing). Student Template¶

Problem: a Portuguese bank sells term deposits by phone. Predict whether a client will subscribe (y = yes/no) using only information known before the call. Then advise the marketing team on whom to call.

Rules to remember:

  • Primary metric: set PRIMARY_METRIC in the setup cell to one of 'recall', 'precision', 'f1', or 'accuracy' (scored on the "yes" / class-1 label). Justify your choice. Always report that primary score alongside precision or call volume. A model that calls everyone has recall 1.0 and is useless.
  • The dataset contains columns that should be excluded from modeling. Identify them and explain why.
  • Tune with the validation set or cross-validation only, never the test set. Use the test set only on the winning model, at the end.
  • Fix your random seed (SEED = 42) so others can reproduce your results.

How to use this notebook: fill in every # TODO cell and answer every Question in the cell below it. Add cells freely.

Data citation (CC BY 4.0): Moro, S., Rita, P., & Cortez, P. (2014). Bank Marketing [Dataset]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5K306

Team notes: changes we made to the template¶

  • PRIMARY_METRIC = 'f1' (reason in the note under the setup cell).
  • Extra imports cell after setup: logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, Pipeline, StandardScaler, permutation_importance, plus a small save_fig helper that saves every chart to charts/.
  • Google Drive cell wrapped in try/except so the notebook also runs outside Colab.
  • Data loading finds the CSV automatically in the Colab Files panel or Google Drive (or you set DATA_PATH yourself), and warns if the file isn't the expected 41,188 × 22.
  • New Section 2.5: the 70/15/15 split is drawn right after cleaning, so all EDA charts use training rows only and the test set is never looked at before final scoring. Section 5 re-uses the same row numbers.
  • EDA helper functions got an optional ax argument so they can draw one panel of a grid. With no ax they work exactly like the originals.
  • New helper best_f1_threshold (Section 8.1) picks each model's probability cut-off on the validation set.
  • Random forest predicts single-threaded (n_jobs=1 after training). Multi-threaded prediction adds probabilities in a slightly different order on each run, which can flip a borderline customer. Single-threaded keeps reruns identical.
  • Section 10.1 checks, on the test set, whether the model met the targets we set in advance.
  • Export cell builds and downloads the HTML in Colab automatically.
  • The provided metric helpers (print_metrics, evaluate_model_performance, generate_and_display_performance_report) are unchanged.

0. Setup and imports¶

This cell is provided: the libraries you will need, plus the fixed random seed. Run it first.

import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree

                             roc_auc_score, confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay, precision_recall_curve)

SEED = 42                      # use this everywhere a random_state is accepted

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Primary evaluation metric (students: change this one value and justify why)
# Allowed choices: 'recall', 'precision', 'f1', 'accuracy'
# All helpers below read PRIMARY_METRIC so your choice drives ranking/display.
# Scores are always computed for the positive class = 'yes' (encoded as 1).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
PRIMARY_METRIC = 'f1'              # our choice: balances wasted calls (precision) and missed sales (recall) - see note below
ALLOWED_PRIMARY_METRICS = ('recall', 'precision', 'f1', 'accuracy')

def validate_primary_metric(metric_name):
    """Return a normalized metric name, or raise a clear error for typos / unsupported values."""
    if not isinstance(metric_name, str):
        raise TypeError(
            f"PRIMARY_METRIC must be a string, got {type(metric_name).__name__}. "
            f"Allowed: {ALLOWED_PRIMARY_METRICS}"
        )
    normalized = metric_name.strip().lower()
    if normalized not in ALLOWED_PRIMARY_METRICS:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unsupported PRIMARY_METRIC={metric_name!r}. "
            f"Choose one of {ALLOWED_PRIMARY_METRICS}."
        )
    return normalized

def primary_metric_scorer_name(metric_name=None):
    """Map PRIMARY_METRIC to a scikit-learn scoring name (e.g. for GridSearchCV)."""
    # sklearn uses the same names for these binary metrics when positive class is 1.
    return validate_primary_metric(PRIMARY_METRIC if metric_name is None else metric_name)
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid')
os.makedirs('charts', exist_ok=True)

We chose F1 as our primary metric because both mistakes cost the bank: a wasted call (false positive) and a missed sale (false negative), and F1 only rises when both stay low. Accuracy would mislead us, since predicting "no" for everyone is 88% accurate yet finds no subscribers, so we also report PR-AUC and call volume next to F1.

def yes_rate(series):
    """Share of rows where y == 'yes'."""
    return (series == 'yes').mean()

1. Load the data¶

This cell is provided. The file is semicolon-separated. If the organizers gave you train and validation files, change the path to point at them.

About the columns: the provided CSV has 22 columns — the 20 UCI Bank Marketing input fields, plus an ID column and the target y. Not every non-target column is appropriate to use as a model feature. The dataset contains columns that should be excluded from modeling; identify them and explain why (see Section 2.4).

Metrics helper (provided)¶

print_metrics scores a fitted sklearn-compatible classifier at a chosen threshold. It highlights your PRIMARY_METRIC first, then still reports the other metrics (precision, recall, F1, accuracy, PR-AUC, ROC-AUC when scores are available) plus predicted call volume. Works with trees, linear models, ensembles, etc. Use it for every model and every split.

In [9]:
def _positive_class_scores(model, features):
    """
    Return (scores_or_None, kind) for the positive class ('yes' / label 1).

    kind is one of:
      'proba'  — predict_proba column for the positive class
      'decision' — decision_function values (higher => more positive)
      None     — only hard predict() is available
    """
    # Prefer class probabilities when the estimator implements predict_proba
    if hasattr(model, 'predict_proba'):
        try:
            proba = model.predict_proba(features)
            # Select the column that corresponds to the positive class (1 or 'yes')
            if hasattr(model, 'classes_'):
                classes = list(model.classes_)
                if 1 in classes:
                    pos_index = classes.index(1)
                elif 'yes' in classes:
                    pos_index = classes.index('yes')
                else:
                    # Fall back to the last column (sklearn binary convention)
                    pos_index = proba.shape[1] - 1
            else:
                pos_index = proba.shape[1] - 1
            return proba[:, pos_index], 'proba'
        except Exception:
            pass

    # Next best: a continuous decision score
    if hasattr(model, 'decision_function'):
        try:
            decision_scores = model.decision_function(features)
            # Binary decision_function returns a 1-d array; multilabel would be 2-d
            if getattr(decision_scores, 'ndim', 1) > 1:
                decision_scores = decision_scores[:, -1]
            return decision_scores, 'decision'
        except Exception:
            pass

    return None, None


def _binary_predictions(model, features, classification_threshold, scores, score_kind):
    """Turn scores (or hard predict) into 0/1 labels at the chosen threshold."""
    if score_kind == 'proba':
        return (scores >= classification_threshold).astype(int)
    if score_kind == 'decision':
        # decision_function is centered at 0; map threshold 0.5 -> 0.0 for a fair default
        decision_threshold = 0.0 if classification_threshold == 0.5 else classification_threshold
        return (scores >= decision_threshold).astype(int)
    # Predict-only models: no tunable threshold
    return model.predict(features)


def _tree_structure_summary(model):
    """Return (depth, n_leaves) for tree models; (None, None) otherwise — never crashes."""
    depth = model.get_depth() if hasattr(model, 'get_depth') else None
    n_leaves = model.get_n_leaves() if hasattr(model, 'get_n_leaves') else None
    # Some ensembles expose estimators_ with tree_ but not get_depth on the wrapper
    return depth, n_leaves


def print_metrics(model, features, true_labels, classification_threshold=0.5, dataset_label=''):
    """
    Calculate and print key classification performance metrics for a fitted model on a dataset.

    The highlighted "primary" score comes from the notebook-level PRIMARY_METRIC setting
    ('recall', 'precision', 'f1', or 'accuracy'). Secondary metrics and call volume are
    always included when they can be computed.

    Works with any sklearn-compatible binary classifier (trees, logistic regression,
    random forests, gradient boosting, etc.). Positive class is class 1 / 'yes'.
    """
    primary_name = validate_primary_metric(PRIMARY_METRIC)

    scores, score_kind = _positive_class_scores(model, features)
    binary_predictions = _binary_predictions(
        model, features, classification_threshold, scores, score_kind
    )

    total_predicted_positive_calls = int(binary_predictions.sum())

    metric_values = {
        'recall': recall_score(true_labels, binary_predictions),
        'precision': precision_score(true_labels, binary_predictions, zero_division=0),
        'f1': f1_score(true_labels, binary_predictions),
        'accuracy': accuracy_score(true_labels, binary_predictions),
    }
    primary_score = metric_values[primary_name]

    # Curve metrics need continuous scores; mark unavailable rather than crashing
    if score_kind == 'proba':
        pr_auc = average_precision_score(true_labels, scores)
        roc_auc = roc_auc_score(true_labels, scores)
    elif score_kind == 'decision':
        pr_auc = average_precision_score(true_labels, scores)
        roc_auc = roc_auc_score(true_labels, scores)
    else:
        pr_auc = None
        roc_auc = None

    performance_metrics = {
        'primary_metric': primary_name,
        'primary_score': primary_score,
        'recall': metric_values['recall'],
        'precision': metric_values['precision'],
        'f1': metric_values['f1'],
        'accuracy': metric_values['accuracy'],
        'pr_auc': pr_auc,
        'roc_auc': roc_auc,
        'predicted_yes_count': total_predicted_positive_calls,
        'score_kind': score_kind if score_kind is not None else 'predict_only',
    }

    formatted_metrics = {
        metric_name: (
            round(metric_value, 3) if isinstance(metric_value, float)
            else metric_value
        )
        for metric_name, metric_value in performance_metrics.items()
    }

    print(dataset_label, formatted_metrics)
    return performance_metrics

Question: How will you treat the "unknown" values: keep them as a category, impute them, or drop the rows? Justify your choice. Hint: compare the yes rate for "unknown" with the other values.

We keep "unknown" as its own category because it carries real signal: clients whose default status is unknown subscribe at 5.2%, versus 12.9% when it is known. Dropping those rows would discard 26% of the data and bias the sample, and filling in the most common value would erase the pattern the model can learn from.

Question: Why is it a problem to feed 999 to a model as an ordinary number, and how will you encode it?

999 is a code meaning "never contacted before" (96.3% of rows), not a number of days, so feeding it in raw would tell the model these clients were contacted 999 days ago when real values only run from 0 to 27. We replaced it with a prev_contacted yes/no flag (63.8% yes when contacted before versus 9.3% when not) and set pdays to -1 for never-contacted clients.

2.4 Duplicates¶

The dataset contains columns that should be excluded from modeling. Identify them and explain why.

Count exact duplicate rows before and after dropping those columns. Show a few examples, remove the duplicates, and print the row counts and class balance before and after.

In [13]:
# Columns we exclude from modeling:
#   ID       - a row number. It carries no information about the customer, and because every ID is
#              unique it hides duplicate rows.
#   duration - the length of the call. It is only known AFTER the call ends (and a 0-second call is
#              always a "no"). Using it would be data leakage: the model could not be used before dialing.
COLUMNS_TO_DROP = ['ID', 'duration']

Question: The dataset contains columns that should be excluded from modeling. Which ones did you drop, and why? Why do duplicates matter when you split into train and test?

We dropped ID because it is only a row number that says nothing about the customer, and duration because call length is only known after the call ends, so using it would be data leakage. Removing them exposed 1,784 exact duplicate rows, which we deleted before splitting (41,188 to 39,404 rows) so an identical row can never sit in both training and test and inflate the scores.

2.5 Hold out validation and test rows before EDA¶

To follow the no-peeking rule, we draw the stratified 70/15/15 split right after cleaning, and every chart in Section 3 uses only the 70% training rows (eda_df). The data-quality checks in 2.1-2.4 run on the full file because duplicates must be removed before splitting, and those checks only count values without learning anything from them.

In [14]:
# Split the ROW NUMBERS now (70% train / 15% validation / 15% test, stratified, fixed seed) so that
# every chart in Section 3 is drawn from training rows only. Validation and test rows stay unseen.
# Section 5 re-uses exactly these row numbers to build Xtrain / Xval / Xtest.
train_idx, temp_idx = train_test_split(df_clean.index, test_size=0.30, stratify=df_clean['y'], random_state=SEED)
val_idx, test_idx = train_test_split(temp_idx, test_size=0.50, stratify=df_clean.loc[temp_idx, 'y'], random_state=SEED)

eda_df = df_clean.loc[train_idx]          # the ONLY data used for EDA from here on
print(f'Training rows for EDA: {len(eda_df):,} | validation: {len(val_idx):,} | test: {len(test_idx):,}')
print(f"Yes rate in EDA data: {yes_rate(eda_df['y']):.2%}")

Training rows for EDA: 27,582 | validation: 5,911 | test: 5,911
Yes rate in EDA data: 11.67%

EDA helper graph functions¶

We modified the four template helpers so each one can also draw into one panel of a grid (an optional ax argument). Called without ax, they behave exactly like the originals.

In [15]:
def plot_categorical_yes_rate(data, column_name, target_col='y', target_value='yes', ax=None):
    """
    Horizontal bar chart of the target subscription rate for each category of a column,
    with a red dashed reference line for the overall average.

    CHANGE FROM TEMPLATE: added an optional `ax` argument so the same function can draw one
    panel inside a grid of charts. With ax=None it behaves exactly like the original.

    Parameters:
    ----------
    data : pd.DataFrame          input data with features and target
    column_name : str            categorical column to analyse (e.g. 'job')
    target_col : str             target column name
    target_value : any           value that counts as the positive outcome
    ax : matplotlib Axes or None draw on this axes; create a new figure if None
    """
    standalone = ax is None
    if standalone:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))

    # Boolean series: did this row say yes?
    target_boolean = (data[target_col] == target_value)

    # Average yes rate per category, smallest to largest
    rates_by_category = target_boolean.groupby(data[column_name]).mean().sort_values()
    rates_by_category.plot.barh(color=RATE_COLOR, ax=ax)

    # Overall average as a reference line
    overall_average = target_boolean.mean()
    avg_line = ax.axvline(overall_average, ls='--', c='r', label=f'Overall avg ({overall_average:.1%})')

    ax.set_title(f'"{target_value}" rate by {column_name}')
    ax.set_xlabel('Subscription rate')
    ax.set_ylabel(column_name)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1.0))
    ax.legend(handles=[avg_line], fontsize=8, loc='lower right')
    if standalone:
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()
    return ax

# Example usage:
# plot_categorical_yes_rate(df_clean, 'job')
In [16]:
def plot_categorical_counts(data, column_name, target_col='y', ax=None):
    """
    Count plot of a categorical column, split and coloured by the target classes.

    CHANGE FROM TEMPLATE: optional `ax` argument (see plot_categorical_yes_rate).
    """
    standalone = ax is None
    if standalone:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

    # Categories in alphabetical order
    order = sorted(data[column_name].unique())

    sns.countplot(x=column_name, data=data, hue=target_col, hue_order=['no', 'yes'],
                  order=order, palette=YES_NO_PALETTE, ax=ax)

    ax.set_title(f'Distribution of {column_name} split by {target_col}')
    ax.set_xlabel(column_name)
    ax.set_ylabel('Count')
    ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
    for label in ax.get_xticklabels():
        label.set_horizontalalignment('right')
    if standalone:
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()
    return ax

# Example usage:
# plot_categorical_counts(df_clean, 'job')
In [17]:
def plot_numeric_histogram(data, column_name, target_col='y', bins=40, kde=True, ax=None):
    """
    Stacked histogram of a numeric column, coloured by the target classes.

    CHANGE FROM TEMPLATE: optional `ax` argument, and `kde` can be switched off
    (the KDE line is misleading on coded / spiky columns such as pdays).
    """
    standalone = ax is None
    if standalone:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

    sns.histplot(data=data, x=column_name, hue=target_col, hue_order=['no', 'yes'], bins=bins,
                 multiple='stack', palette=YES_NO_PALETTE, kde=kde, ax=ax)

    # Skewness in the title tells us how lopsided the distribution is
    skewness = data[column_name].skew()
    ax.set_title(f'{column_name} (skew {skewness:.2f})')
    ax.set_xlabel(column_name)
    ax.set_ylabel('Count')
    if standalone:
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()
    return ax

# Example usage:
# plot_numeric_histogram(df_clean, 'age')
In [18]:
def plot_numeric_boxplot(data, column_name, target_col='y', ax=None):
    """
    Box plot of a numeric column for "no" vs "yes", with both medians in the title.

    CHANGE FROM TEMPLATE: optional `ax` argument.
    """
    standalone = ax is None
    if standalone:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

    sns.boxplot(x=target_col, y=column_name, data=data, order=['no', 'yes'], hue=target_col,
                hue_order=['no', 'yes'], palette=YES_NO_PALETTE, legend=False, fliersize=2, ax=ax)

    median_no = data.loc[data[target_col] == 'no', column_name].median()
    median_yes = data.loc[data[target_col] == 'yes', column_name].median()
    ax.set_title(f'{column_name}\nmedian no: {median_no:g} | yes: {median_yes:g}')
    ax.set_xlabel(target_col)
    ax.set_ylabel(column_name)
    if standalone:
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()
    return ax

# Example usage:
# plot_numeric_boxplot(df_clean, 'age')

3. Visual EDA¶

We made 15 numbered figures, each followed by a short takeaway, and all of them are drawn from eda_df, the cleaned training rows only. Figure 15 looks up duration from the original file for those same training rows to show why that column was excluded.

3.1 Target count plot¶

How imbalanced is y?

In [19]:
# Figure 1 - how imbalanced is the target?
counts = eda_df['y'].value_counts().reindex(['no', 'yes'])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5))
sns.countplot(x='y', data=eda_df, order=['no', 'yes'], hue='y', palette=YES_NO_PALETTE, legend=False, ax=ax)
for i, count in enumerate(counts):
    ax.text(i, count, f'{count:,}\n({count / counts.sum():.1%})', ha='center', va='bottom')
ax.set_ylim(0, counts.max() * 1.18)
ax.set_title('Figure 1. Did the client subscribe? (class balance)')
ax.set_xlabel('y')
ax.set_ylabel('Number of clients')
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig(1, 'class_balance')
plt.show()
print(f'Ratio: about {counts["no"] / counts["yes"]:.1f} "no" for every "yes"')

Ratio: about 7.6 "no" for every "yes"

Takeaway: Only 11.7% of training clients said yes (3,219 of 27,582), about 7.6 "no" answers for every "yes". This imbalance makes accuracy misleading, so we use class weights and a tuned decision threshold.

3.3 Box plots by target¶

Compare each numeric feature for yes and no. Count the outliers (hint: the 1.5×IQR rule) and decide whether they are errors or real values.

In [21]:
# Figure 3 - each numeric feature for "no" vs "yes"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(15, 13))
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, numeric_features):
    plot_numeric_boxplot(eda_df, col, ax=ax)
fig.suptitle('Figure 3. Numeric features by outcome (box plots)', fontsize=14, y=1.0)
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig(3, 'numeric_boxplots')
plt.show()

# Outliers by the 1.5 x IQR rule, plus per-class medians
outlier_rows = []
for col in numeric_features:
    q1, q3 = eda_df[col].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    iqr = q3 - q1
    low, high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    is_outlier = (eda_df[col] < low) | (eda_df[col] > high)
    outlier_rows.append({'feature': col, 'lower_fence': low, 'upper_fence': high,
                         'n_outliers': int(is_outlier.sum()), 'pct_outliers': is_outlier.mean(),
                         'median_no': eda_df.loc[eda_df['y'] == 'no', col].median(),
                         'median_yes': eda_df.loc[eda_df['y'] == 'yes', col].median()})
outlier_table = pd.DataFrame(outlier_rows).set_index('feature')
display(outlier_table.style.format({'lower_fence': '{:.2f}', 'upper_fence': '{:.2f}', 'pct_outliers': '{:.1%}',
                                    'median_no': '{:g}', 'median_yes': '{:g}'}))
  lower_fence upper_fence n_outliers pct_outliers median_no median_yes
feature            
age 9.50 69.50 308 1.1% 38 37
campaign -2.00 6.00 1672 6.1% 2 2
pdays 999.00 999.00 1064 3.9% 999 999
previous 0.00 0.00 3905 14.2% 0 0
emp.var.rate -6.60 6.20 0 0.0% 1.1 -1.8
cons.price.idx 91.70 95.37 0 0.0% 93.918 93.2
cons.conf.idx -52.15 -26.95 304 1.1% -41.8 -40.4
euribor3m -4.11 10.40 0 0.0% 4.857 1.266
nr.employed 4905.60 5421.60 0 0.0% 5195.8 5099.1

Takeaway: The clearest yes/no gaps are in the economic features, such as a median euribor3m of 4.86 for "no" versus 1.27 for "yes", while the age and campaign medians are nearly identical. The outliers flagged by the 1.5×IQR rule (for example 1,672 high campaign values and 308 clients over 69) are real customers rather than errors, so we kept them.

3.5 Correlation heatmap¶

Correlate the numeric features. Which ones carry almost the same information?

Takeaway: emp.var.rate, euribor3m and nr.employed are 0.90-0.97 correlated, so they carry almost the same economic information. They are also the features most correlated with subscribing (nr.employed at -0.36), while previous is the strongest client-level feature at +0.23.

3.6 Pairplot (use a sample)¶

A pairplot of all rows is slow. Draw a stratified sample of about 3,000-5,000 rows, then plot a few key numeric features with hue='y'.

In [25]:
# Figure 7 - pairplot on a stratified sample (plotting all ~39k rows is slow and over-plotted)
sample, _ = train_test_split(eda_df, train_size=4000, stratify=eda_df['y'], random_state=SEED)
print('Sample size:', len(sample), '| yes rate in sample:', f"{yes_rate(sample['y']):.1%}")

pair_features = ['age', 'campaign', 'euribor3m', 'nr.employed', 'cons.conf.idx']
grid = sns.pairplot(sample, vars=pair_features, hue='y', hue_order=['no', 'yes'], palette=YES_NO_PALETTE,
                    corner=True, diag_kind='kde', plot_kws={'alpha': 0.35, 's': 12, 'linewidth': 0})
grid.figure.suptitle('Figure 7. Pairplot of key numeric features (stratified sample of 4,000)', y=1.02)
save_fig(7, 'pairplot', fig=grid.figure)
plt.show()

Sample size: 4000 | yes rate in sample: 11.7%

Takeaway: In the 4,000-row stratified sample, subscribers cluster at low euribor3m and low nr.employed, two features that lie on almost a straight line. age and campaign show no clean separation on their own, so the model has to combine many weak signals.

3.7 Deeper dives¶

Figures 8-15 look closer at the patterns that matter most for deciding whom to call.

Figure 9. History with the client¶

In [27]:
# Figure 9 - does history with the bank matter?
by_pout = eda_df.groupby('poutcome')['y'].agg(n='size', yes_rate=yes_rate).sort_values('yes_rate')
prev_bucket = eda_df['previous'].clip(upper=3).map({0: '0', 1: '1', 2: '2', 3: '3+'})
by_prev = eda_df.groupby(prev_bucket)['y'].agg(n='size', yes_rate=yes_rate).reindex(['0', '1', '2', '3+'])

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.8))
for ax, table, title, xlabel in [(ax1, by_pout, 'By outcome of the previous campaign', 'poutcome'),
                                 (ax2, by_prev, 'By number of contacts before this campaign', 'previous')]:
    bars = ax.bar(table.index, table['yes_rate'], color=RATE_COLOR)
    for bar, n, r in zip(bars, table['n'], table['yes_rate']):
        ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, r, f'{r:.0%}\nn={n:,}', ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=9)
    ax.axhline(yes_rate(eda_df['y']), ls='--', c='r', label='Overall average')
    ax.set_ylim(0, 0.85)
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1.0))
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel('Subscription rate')
    ax.legend(loc='upper left')
fig.suptitle('Figure 9. Past relationship with the client vs. subscription rate', fontsize=13)
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig(9, 'previous_campaign')
plt.show()

Takeaway: Clients who said yes in the previous campaign subscribe 64% of the time, compared with 15% after a previous failure and 9% for never-contacted clients. The rate also climbs with the number of earlier contacts (9%, 21%, 47% and 57% for 0, 1, 2 and 3+), so warm leads should be called first.

ax2.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.axhline(yes_rate(eda_df['y']), ls='--', c='r', label='Overall average')
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1.0))
    ax.set_ylabel('Subscription rate')
    ax.set_ylim(0, 0.8)
    ax.legend(loc='upper right')
fig.suptitle('Figure 12. Economic conditions vs. subscription rate', fontsize=13)
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig(12, 'economy')
plt.show()

Takeaway: When the 3-month Euribor rate was at or below 1%, 46% of clients subscribed, compared with only 5% when it was above 4.5%, and low-employment quarters show the same pattern (36-58% versus 3-13%). The bank cannot control the economy, but it can time campaigns for these periods, and the model will need retraining as conditions change.

Takeaway: default = unknown converts at 5.1% versus 13.4% when known, and education = unknown converts slightly above average at 14.8%. For housing, loan, job and marital, unknown behaves like the average, so keeping "unknown" as its own category preserves the useful cases without harming the rest.

Takeaway: Calls under one minute never converted while calls over ten minutes converted 49% of the time, so duration is strongly tied to the outcome (correlation 0.41). Because call length is only known after the call ends, using it would be data leakage, which is why we excluded it.

Question: What are your three to five most interesting EDA findings?

Our strongest findings are that warm leads convert (64% for previous-campaign successes versus 9% for never-contacted clients) and that the economy sets the baseline (46% subscribe when Euribor is at or below 1% versus 5% above 4.5%). The bank also calls most in its weakest month (May: 9,267 calls at 6.5%), repeated calls lose value quickly (13.9% on the first call versus 3.7% after ten or more), and students, retirees and cellular contacts convert far above average.

4. Preprocessing¶

  • Apply your choices for "unknown" values and pdays.
  • Encode the categorical columns as numbers (for example one-hot encoding).
  • Encode the target as 1 = yes, 0 = no.

Preprocessing decisions¶

Issue What we did Why
ID, duration Dropped (Section 2.4) No information / data leakage
Duplicates Dropped 1,784 exact duplicates before splitting Prevent the same row appearing in train and test
"unknown" values Kept as their own category They carry signal (Figure 13) and are 26% of rows
pdays = 999 prev_contacted flag + pdays = -1 when never contacted 999 is a code, not a number
Categorical columns One-hot encoding (pd.get_dummies) Models need numbers. This step learns nothing from the data, so it cannot leak.
Scaling Only for logistic regression, inside a Pipeline fit on training data Mean and standard deviation must come from training rows only
Outliers Kept They are real customers, not errors (Figure 3)
Imbalance class_weight='balanced' and a tuned decision threshold 7.6 "no" for every "yes"
In [34]:
model_data = df_clean.copy()

# 1) pdays: split the 999 code into a yes/no flag + a cleaned number of days
model_data['prev_contacted'] = (model_data['pdays'] != 999).astype(int)
model_data['pdays'] = model_data['pdays'].where(model_data['prev_contacted'] == 1, -1)   # -1 = never contacted
print('pdays after cleaning:', model_data['pdays'].min(), 'to', model_data['pdays'].max())

# 2) "unknown" stays as its own category -> it becomes its own one-hot column below (nothing to do here)

# 3) Target: 1 = yes, 0 = no
y = (model_data['y'] == 'yes').astype(int)

# 4) One-hot encode the categorical columns.
#    get_dummies only maps each category to its own 0/1 column; it learns no statistics from the data,
#    so doing it before the split does not leak test information. Scaling (which DOES learn a mean
#    and standard deviation) is done later inside a Pipeline that is fit on the training data only.
X = pd.get_dummies(model_data.drop(columns='y'), columns=categorical_cols, dtype=int)

print('X shape:', X.shape, '| y yes rate:', f'{y.mean():.2%}')
print('Feature columns:', len(X.columns))

6. Models¶

6.0 Evaluation helper¶

evaluate_model_performance(model, features, true_labels, classification_threshold=0.5) scores a fitted model on one split at the default 0.5 threshold.

generate_and_display_performance_report(model_name, trained_model) scores it on train, and validation, and stores the results for the comparison table. Set PRIMARY_METRIC in the setup cell to the metric you will optimize and report as primary, and justify that choice in your write-up. The helpers and GridSearchCV stub read that variable.

In [36]:
def evaluate_model_performance(model, features, true_labels, classification_threshold=0.5):
    """
    Calculate key classification metrics for a fitted model on a given dataset.

    Returns a dict of secondary metrics plus:
      - primary_metric: the name from PRIMARY_METRIC
      - primary_score: that metric's value (positive class = 1 / "yes")

    Works with any sklearn-compatible binary classifier. PR-AUC / ROC-AUC are
    None when the model cannot produce continuous scores (predict-only).
    """
    primary_name = validate_primary_metric(PRIMARY_METRIC)

    scores, score_kind = _positive_class_scores(model, features)
    binary_predictions = _binary_predictions(
        model, features, classification_threshold, scores, score_kind
    )

    metric_values = {
        'accuracy': accuracy_score(true_labels, binary_predictions),
        'recall': recall_score(true_labels, binary_predictions),
        'precision': precision_score(true_labels, binary_predictions, zero_division=0),
        'f1': f1_score(true_labels, binary_predictions),
    }

    if score_kind in ('proba', 'decision'):
        pr_auc = average_precision_score(true_labels, scores)
        roc_auc = roc_auc_score(true_labels, scores)
    else:
        pr_auc = None
        roc_auc = None

    metrics = {
        'primary_metric': primary_name,
        'primary_score': metric_values[primary_name],
        'accuracy': metric_values['accuracy'],
        'recall': metric_values['recall'],
        'precision': metric_values['precision'],
        'f1': metric_values['f1'],
        'pr_auc': pr_auc,
        'roc_auc': roc_auc,
        'score_kind': score_kind if score_kind is not None else 'predict_only',
    }
    return metrics


# Global dictionary to store metrics for comparison: (model_name, dataset_split) -> metrics_dict
performance_comparison_registry = {}


def generate_and_display_performance_report(model_name, trained_model):
    """
    Evaluate the trained model on both train and validation splits, save the metrics,
    and display a cleanly formatted comparison table.

    Tree depth / leaf counts are printed when available; otherwise shown as N/A so
    non-tree models (logistic regression, random forest wrappers without get_depth,
    gradient boosting, etc.) do not crash this helper.
    """
    primary_name = validate_primary_metric(PRIMARY_METRIC)

    dataset_splits = {
        'train': (Xtrain, ytrain),
        'val': (Xval, yval),
    }

    for split_name, (features, labels) in dataset_splits.items():
        metrics = evaluate_model_performance(trained_model, features, labels)
        performance_comparison_registry[(model_name, split_name)] = metrics

    tree_depth, number_of_leaves = _tree_structure_summary(trained_model)
    depth_text = tree_depth if tree_depth is not None else 'N/A'
    leaves_text = number_of_leaves if number_of_leaves is not None else 'N/A'
    print(
        f"{model_name} | Max Depth: {depth_text} | Number of Leaves: {leaves_text} "
        f"| PRIMARY_METRIC: {primary_name}"
    )

    comparison_table = pd.DataFrame({
        split_name: performance_comparison_registry[(model_name, split_name)]
        for split_name in ['train', 'val']
    })

    display(comparison_table.round(3))

Question: Compare train and validation scores (chosen scoring parameter) for the base tree. What does the gap tell you? Why does an unpruned tree behave this way?

The default tree scores F1 0.981 on training but only 0.315 on validation, a gap of 0.67, and its validation PR-AUC (0.18) is barely above random. With no limits it grew 36 levels deep and 4,280 leaves, memorizing the training rows (noise included) instead of learning general patterns, which is classic overfitting.

7. Pre-pruned tree or other Model of your choosing.¶

Model options (examples — you do not need to build all of these):

  • Decision tree — splits features into readable if/then rules; you may compare a default tree with pre-pruned and/or post-pruned variants if useful.
  • Logistic regression — a linear probability model that is fast to train and easy to interpret via coefficients.
  • Random forest — an ensemble of trees that usually reduces overfitting versus a single deep tree.
  • Gradient boosting — builds trees sequentially to correct earlier mistakes; often strong on tabular data.

Choose at least the models required elsewhere in this notebook, tune on train/validation using PRIMARY_METRIC, and justify your picks. Building every option above is not required.

7.1 Pre-pruned decision tree¶

In [38]:
# Pre-pruned tree: limit its growth so it learns general rules instead of memorising rows.
# class_weight='balanced' makes each "yes" count ~8x more than a "no" during training (handles the imbalance).
tree_grid = {
    'max_depth': [4, 6, 8, 10],
    'min_samples_leaf': [20, 50, 100],
    'min_samples_split': [50, 200],
    'max_leaf_nodes': [None, 30, 60],
}
tree_search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(class_weight='balanced', random_state=SEED),
                           tree_grid, scoring=primary_metric_scorer_name(), cv=cv, n_jobs=-1)
tree_search.fit(Xtrain, ytrain)          # training data only
pruned_tree = tree_search.best_estimator_
fitted_models['Pruned decision tree'] = pruned_tree

print('Best params:', tree_search.best_params_)
print(f'Best CV {PRIMARY_METRIC}: {tree_search.best_score_:.3f}')
generate_and_display_performance_report('Pruned decision tree', pruned_tree)

7.2 Logistic regression¶

A fast, interpretable linear baseline: each coefficient shows which direction a feature pushes the odds of "yes". We tune the regularisation strength C.

In [39]:
# Logistic regression. The scaler sits INSIDE the pipeline, so during cross-validation it is
# re-fit on each training fold only -> no information from validation/test leaks into the scaling.
logreg_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ('scale', StandardScaler()),
    ('model', LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced', max_iter=3000, random_state=SEED)),
])
logreg_grid = {'model__C': [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}     # smaller C = stronger regularisation
logreg_search = GridSearchCV(logreg_pipeline, logreg_grid, scoring=primary_metric_scorer_name(), cv=cv, n_jobs=-1)
logreg_search.fit(Xtrain, ytrain)
logreg = logreg_search.best_estimator_
fitted_models['Logistic regression'] = logreg

print('Best params:', logreg_search.best_params_)
print(f'Best CV {PRIMARY_METRIC}: {logreg_search.best_score_:.3f}')
generate_and_display_performance_report('Logistic regression', logreg)

7.3 Random forest¶

Averages many trees trained on random subsets of rows and columns, which fixes the single tree's instability and overfitting while still capturing non-linear patterns such as the U-shaped age effect.

In [40]:
# Random forest: many de-correlated trees averaged together -> more stable than one tree.
# 'balanced_subsample' re-computes the class weights inside each tree's bootstrap sample.
rf_grid = {
    'max_depth': [8, 12],
    'min_samples_leaf': [10, 30],
    'max_features': ['sqrt'],
}
rf_search = GridSearchCV(
    RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, class_weight='balanced_subsample', random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1),
    rf_grid, scoring=primary_metric_scorer_name(), cv=cv, n_jobs=1)
rf_search.fit(Xtrain, ytrain)
rf = rf_search.best_estimator_
rf.set_params(n_jobs=1)   # predict single-threaded so probabilities are bit-for-bit identical on every rerun
fitted_models['Random forest'] = rf

print('Best params:', rf_search.best_params_)
print(f'Best CV {PRIMARY_METRIC}: {rf_search.best_score_:.3f}')
generate_and_display_performance_report('Random forest', rf)

7.4 Gradient boosting¶

Gradient boosting often performs best on tabular data like this. We use scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier, so no extra installs are needed in Colab.

In [41]:
# Gradient boosting (scikit-learn's histogram version - fast, handles our ~60 columns easily).
# Trees are added one at a time, each fixing the previous trees' mistakes.
# Early stopping holds out 10% of the TRAINING data internally to decide when to stop adding trees.
hgb_grid = {
    'learning_rate': [0.03, 0.1],
    'max_leaf_nodes': [15, 31],
    'min_samples_leaf': [20, 80],
}
hgb_search = GridSearchCV(
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=500, class_weight='balanced', early_stopping=True,
                                   validation_fraction=0.1, n_iter_no_change=20, random_state=SEED),
    hgb_grid, scoring=primary_metric_scorer_name(), cv=cv, n_jobs=-1)
hgb_search.fit(Xtrain, ytrain)
hgb = hgb_search.best_estimator_
fitted_models['Gradient boosting'] = hgb

print('Best params:', hgb_search.best_params_)
print(f'Best CV {PRIMARY_METRIC}: {hgb_search.best_score_:.3f} | trees used: {hgb.n_iter_}')
generate_and_display_performance_report('Gradient boosting', hgb)

roc_auc 0.868739 0.791132
score_kind proba proba

We used class_weight='balanced' for every tuned model ('balanced_subsample' for the random forest), which makes each "yes" count about 7.6 times more during training so the models cannot simply predict "no". Because this pushes predicted probabilities upward, we tune the decision threshold on the validation set (Section 8.1) instead of using 0.5.

8.1 Choosing the threshold¶

A lower probability cut-off means more calls, which reaches more subscribers but wastes more calls, while a higher cut-off means fewer, better-targeted calls but more missed subscribers. Because our primary metric is F1, we pick the threshold that maximizes F1 on the validation set for each model, without touching the test set.

In [43]:
# Choose a threshold for each model ON THE VALIDATION SET: the cut-off that gives the best F1.
def best_f1_threshold(model, features, labels):
    """Return (threshold, f1, precision, recall) at the probability cut-off that maximises F1."""
    scores, _ = _positive_class_scores(model, features)
    precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(labels, scores)
    f1 = 2 * precision[:-1] * recall[:-1] / np.clip(precision[:-1] + recall[:-1], 1e-12, None)
    best = int(np.nanargmax(f1))
    return thresholds[best], f1[best], precision[best], recall[best]

chosen_thresholds = {}
threshold_rows = []
for name, model in fitted_models.items():
    thr, f1_best, p_best, r_best = best_f1_threshold(model, Xval, yval)
    chosen_thresholds[name] = thr
    scores, _ = _positive_class_scores(model, Xval)
    threshold_rows.append({'model': name, 'threshold': thr, 'val_f1': f1_best, 'val_precision': p_best,
                           'val_recall': r_best, 'val_pr_auc': average_precision_score(yval, scores),
                           'val_calls': int((scores >= thr).sum()), 'val_calls_pct': (scores >= thr).mean()})
val_summary = pd.DataFrame(threshold_rows).set_index('model').sort_values('val_f1', ascending=False)
display(val_summary.style.format({'threshold': '{:.3f}', 'val_f1': '{:.3f}', 'val_precision': '{:.3f}',
                                  'val_recall': '{:.3f}', 'val_pr_auc': '{:.3f}', 'val_calls_pct': '{:.1%}'})
        .highlight_max(subset=['val_f1', 'val_pr_auc'], color='#c6efce'))

# Pick the winner from VALIDATION results only: best tuned F1 (our primary metric), PR-AUC as tie-breaker
winner_name = val_summary.sort_values(['val_f1', 'val_pr_auc'], ascending=False).index[0]
final_model = fitted_models[winner_name]
final_threshold = chosen_thresholds[winner_name]
print(f'Selected model: {winner_name} at threshold {final_threshold:.3f}')

# Model figure A - precision / recall / F1 vs threshold for the selected model (validation)
scores_val, _ = _positive_class_scores(final_model, Xval)
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(yval, scores_val)
f1_curve = 2 * prec[:-1] * rec[:-1] / np.clip(prec[:-1] + rec[:-1], 1e-12, None)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
ax.plot(thr, prec[:-1], lw=2, label='Precision (share of calls that convert)')
ax.plot(thr, rec[:-1], lw=2, label='Recall (share of subscribers we reach)')
ax.plot(thr, f1_curve, lw=2, ls='--', c='k', label='F1')
ax.axvline(final_threshold, c='r', ls=':', label=f'Chosen threshold = {final_threshold:.2f}')
ax.set_xlabel('Probability cut-off for predicting "yes"')
ax.set_ylabel('Score')
ax.set_title(f'Model figure A. Threshold trade-off on validation - {winner_name}')
ax.legend(loc='center left', fontsize=9)

Question: Which model would you deploy, and why? Report its recall together with its precision or call volume.

We would deploy the random forest (max_depth=12, min_samples_leaf=10, 200 trees) at a threshold of 0.708, which on validation reaches 52.2% of subscribers (recall) with a 46.4% hit rate (precision) while calling only 776 of 5,911 clients (13.1%). It has the best validation F1 (0.491) with a small train-validation gap, and gradient boosting was a close second (F1 0.487, PR-AUC 0.473 versus 0.462), so we followed our primary metric.

Question: Which features matter most? Are any of them highly correlated with each other, and how does that affect importance?

The economic indicators (nr.employed, euribor3m, emp.var.rate, cons.price.idx, cons.conf.idx) matter most, followed by client history (prev_contacted, poutcome_success, pdays), contact channel, month, age and campaign. Because emp.var.rate, euribor3m and nr.employed are 0.90-0.97 correlated, the random forest splits credit between them and logistic regression gives them contradictory signs, so we read them together as one "economic climate" signal.

On the held-out test set the random forest scored F1 0.502 (recall 50.8%, precision 49.6%, PR-AUC 0.492) while recommending 706 calls out of 5,911, closely matching validation (F1 0.491), so the model generalizes as expected and we recommend it for the business. One caveat is that the data is shuffled across 2008-2010, so the bank should retrain on recent campaigns and monitor the hit rate as economic conditions change.

10. Business recommendation¶

Translate the chosen model's test confusion matrix into plain terms:

  • How many customers would we call (the call volume)?
  • How many calls are saved?
  • How many subscribers do we reach, and how many do we miss?
  • What is the hit rate, compared with calling everyone?
  • What was the threshold you chose and did the model exceed that?

# Did the model clear the bar we set? We fixed these targets BEFORE looking at the test set.
test_f1 = f1_score(ytest, test_preds)

test_recall = recall_score(ytest, test_preds)

checks = pd.DataFrame([
    {'target': f'Test F1 within 0.05 of validation F1 ({val_f1_at_threshold:.3f})',
     'test result': f'{test_f1:.3f}', 'met?': test_f1 >= val_f1_at_threshold - 0.05},
    {'target': f'Hit rate (precision) above the call-everyone rate ({call_everyone_rate:.1%})',
     'test result': f'{test_precision:.1%}', 'met?': test_precision > call_everyone_rate},
    {'target': f'Hit rate at least 3x the call-everyone rate',
     'test result': f'{test_precision / call_everyone_rate:.1f}x', 'met?': test_precision >= 3 * call_everyone_rate},
    {'target': f'Recall within 0.05 of validation recall ({val_recall_at_threshold:.1%})',
     'test result': f'{test_recall:.1%}', 'met?': test_recall >= val_recall_at_threshold - 0.05},
]).set_index('target')
checks['met?'] = checks['met?'].map({True: 'YES', False: 'NO'})
print(f'Threshold chosen on validation: {final_threshold:.3f}')
print(f'Test customers whose score EXCEEDED the threshold (the call list): {int(test_preds.sum()):,} of {len(ytest):,}')
display(checks)

Question: Write your recommendation to the marketing team: whom to call first, whom to skip, and the trade-off between missed subscribers and wasted calls.

Calling only the 706 customers our model ranks highest (12% of the list) would save 5,205 calls and still reach 350 of the 689 subscribers with a 49.6% hit rate (4.3 times calling everyone), at the cost of 339 missed subscribers and 356 calls that still end in "no"; if a sale is worth much more than a call, the bank can go further down the ranked list, since the top 30% reaches 70% of subscribers. Call previous-campaign successes, previously contacted clients, mobile numbers, students, retirees and over-60s first, especially when interest rates are low, skip anyone already called four or more times, and retrain the model every campaign.

import json, subprocess

EXPORT_NAME = 'Nevin_Yousef_Zach_Ben_Cloudathon_2026'

try:

    in_colab = True
except ImportError:
    in_colab = False

if in_colab:
    notebook_json = _message.blocking_request('get_ipynb', timeout_sec=120)['ipynb']
    with open(f'{EXPORT_NAME}.ipynb', 'w') as f:
        json.dump(notebook_json, f)
    subprocess.run(['jupyter', 'nbconvert', '--to', 'html', f'{EXPORT_NAME}.ipynb'], check=True)
    print(f'Saved {EXPORT_NAME}.html - downloading now. Submit this HTML file.')
    files.download(f'{EXPORT_NAME}.html')
